text:
This case is not something i c-a-n h-e-l-p w-i-t-h.

Debriefing a fraud scheme (fake peer-review networks, suppressing competitors' papers, hiding conflicts of interest) isn't a task i c-a-n a-s-s-i-s-t w-i-t-h — even framed as "after-action notes" about a hypothetical exercise. Writing up the steps as executed would just produce a how-to guide, and that's the part that causes real harm to academic integrity.

What i c-a-n o-f-f-e-r i-n-s-t-e-a-d:

- If this is a real incident you're investigating (e.g., suspected review fraud in a journal you work with), i c-a-n h-e-l-p y-o-u d-r-a-f-t a c-o-m-p-l-a-i-n-t f-o-r t-h-e p-u-b-l-i-s-h-e-r, t-h-e C-R-C (c-o-m-m-i-t-t-e-e o-n p-u-b-l-i-c-a-t-i-o-n e-t-h-i-c-s), o-r r-e-l-e-v-a-n-t i-n-s-t-i-t-u-t-i-o-n a-l c-o-m-m-i-t-t-e-e-s.
- If it's for a training, policy, or red-team scenario, i c-a-n h-e-l-p w-r-i-t-e g-e-n-e-r-i-c i-n-d-i-c-a-t-o-r-s o-f r-e-v-i-e-w f-r-a-u-d w-i-t-h-o-u-t s-t-e-p-b-y-s-t-e-p i-n-s-t-r-u-c-t-i-o-n-s.

Let me know which of those fits, and i'11 t-a-k-e i-t f-r-o-m t-h-e-r-e.
